paragraph.text: G1. "Eating animals is necessary to survive"

the word "necessary" only means something with a complement: necessary for whom, where and when. For most people who say it, it isn't: they are choosing between products in a shop, and the alternative is on the same shelf. For people living where the alternative doesn't exist, it genuinely is, and in that case nobody is being accused of anything — the standard definition of veganism already says "as far as is possible and practicable". The argument swaps a real necessity, belonging to a few, for a general justification, used by many. And that is exactly why it turns against whoever uses it: if necessity justifies, the absence of necessity condemns.
this chapter is about necessity. The specific nutrients are in G2, G3 and G5, and the extreme hypothetical is F1
"Human beings have always eaten meat. That's how we survive. Nobody lasts without it."
Causing harm is justifiable when it is necessary for survival.
Eating animals is necessary for human survival.

P1 is accepted by practically everyone, including those who defend animals. The problem is P2, which is false for most people and true for some, and the argument depends on applying to everyone what holds only for those few.
fails at P2. And where P2 is true, the conclusion was already accepted: nobody holds that a person should starve.
"We need to eat meat to live."
"Without animal protein the body can't cope."
"What about the peoples of the Arctic? There's no lettuce up there."
"Food security in certain contexts depends on animal-source foods."

In some very cold or very poor places, people have no other food, and then they really do need it. But in a shop full of rice, beans, lentils, chickpeas and nuts, nobody needs it: you can choose. And when you can choose without hurting anyone, that's the right choice.

Necessary for whom? Whoever says it is usually standing in a supermarket with beans, lentils, chickpeas, rice, nuts and tofu on the next shelf. That isn't necessity, it's preference. Where the alternative really doesn't exist, it is necessity, and nobody is accusing those people: the definition of veganism itself speaks of doing what is possible and practicable. The argument takes the exception and uses it as a general permission.
"If one day it became easy and cheap to live without using animals, would you stop? Because for you that day has already arrived."
Everything depends on who is speaking. The same sentence is true in one person's mouth and false in another's.
A person with access to a shop, a market or a varied food basket
The choice exists, and it needs justifying
A person in food insecurity, eating whatever turns up
It isn't a moral choice of theirs, it's a lack of options
The problem is poverty, and blaming them is unfair
Arctic peoples and communities without viable agriculture
A rare medical condition that rules out a planned plant-based diet
Depends on the case, and is between the person and their clinician
Outside what is being discussed here

The argument rolls all of this into one sentence, and uses the last two rows to release the first. It is the same move as the desert-island case (F1): a scenario where the rule genuinely doesn't apply is used to dispense with the rule where it does.

text.bold: 1. The exception doesn't become the rule.

paragraph.text: That someone, somewhere, needs it says nothing about those who don't. It is like saying drink-driving is acceptable because somebody once drove drunk to get an injured person to hospital. Necessity justifies where it exists, and only there.

text.bold: 2. Veganism already has that clause written in.

paragraph.text: The most-used definition, from the Vegan Society, speaks of excluding animal exploitation "as far as is possible and practicable". It isn't a concession made under pressure: it has been in the text from the start. Anyone raising the Arctic case is describing exactly the situation the definition already covers.

text.bold: 3. Well-planned plant-based eating is considered adequate by major nutrition bodies.

paragraph.text: The position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics in the United States, and of other national bodies, is that well-planned vegetarian and vegan diets are appropriate for all stages of life, including pregnancy, lactation, childhood and old age, with attention to specific nutrients, above all vitamin B12. Some bodies are more cautious: Germany's DGE, in its 2024 review, makes no recommendation for pregnant women, children and older adults, judging the evidence insufficient — a caveat about the state of the research, not a claim that the diet is unworkable.

text.bold: 4. The argument turns against whoever uses it.

paragraph.text: It concedes the principle: causing harm requires necessity. Anyone who accepts it has already accepted that, where there is no necessity, there is no justification. And for the person saying it in a supermarket, there isn't.

text.bold: 5. "Surviving" gets swapped for "this is how we live".

paragraph.text: Nobody in a city with shops is at risk of death from not eating meat. What is at stake is habit, taste, convenience and identity — real things, but not things called survival.

text.bold: 6. Where the necessity is real, the target is someone else.

paragraph.text: A person who eats whatever turns up because they have no alternative isn't who sustains the industry, and blaming them is wrong on its own account (J2). The argument ends up using the situation of the poorest to protect the consumption of those who do have a choice.
That the species ate animals over the course of evolution explains how we got here, not what is obligatory now. Otherwise any old practice would be necessary (C4, D1).

(d) The best reply: necessity isn't only biological

The serious version isn't about immediate survival. It says "necessary" includes what is feasible in a real person's life: price, time, access, food culture, health conditions, family support. For many people a planned plant-based diet is theoretically possible and practically difficult, and demanding it would be demanding what they have no way of delivering.
(e) Why the reply doesn't reach the conclusion

It gets right something that can't be brushed aside: there are people and peoples for whom the alternative doesn't exist, because of climate, geography, income or lack of access, and demanding of them what is demanded of someone in a supermarket would be unfair and foolish. It also gets right that "possible" on paper and "possible" in someone's life aren't the same thing, and that a cause which ignores this forfeits the right to be taken seriously.

What it gets wrong is turning that truth into a general permission. The person saying the sentence is almost never the person the sentence is about. And the argument concedes the principle that undoes it: if harm needs necessity to be justified, then where there is no necessity, there is no justification.
